Purpose and Scope of This Document
This document is a structured knowledge base for the Smelter Asset Health Copilot, an AI-driven predictive and
prescriptive maintenance system used at a gold mining smelter plant. It is written to be consumed as a retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG) source: each section is self-contained, uses consistent terminology, and pairs sensor
symptoms with root causes and recommended actions so that a language model can retrieve the most relevant passage
and produce an accurate, actionable maintenance recommendation.
The document supports the end-to-end pipeline shown in the reference architecture:
1. Sensor — Equipment IoT sensors (vibration, temperature, pressure, current, flow, etc.)
2. Snowflake Bronze — raw data ingestion / landing zone
3. Data Cleaning — handling missing values, outliers, duplicates, data quality
4. Feature Engineering — rolling statistics, trends, lag features
5. Anomaly Detection — Isolation Forest (unsupervised ML) combined with statistical rules (thresholds, control limits,
domain/business logic)
6. Anomaly Score — combined ML + rule score
7. LLM Copilot — analyzes context, history, and signals
8. Natural Language / Maintenance Recommendation — human-readable insight, root cause, and
recommendation
9. Dashboard — anomaly overview, insights, recommendations, and history
10. Planner Review — human review of anomaly, insight, and recommended action
11. Approve? — planner decision gate
12. Generate Work Order (if approved) or Dismiss/Monitor (if not)
13. n8n — workflow automation / orchestration
14. SAP PM / CMMS — work order created in the enterprise maintenance system
This knowledge base is the content that powers steps 7 and 8: given an anomaly score and its supporting sensor signals,
the Copilot should be able to identify the most probable failure mode(s), rank them by likelihood, explain the reasoning in
plain language, and propose a specific, prioritized maintenance action — exactly as shown in the dashboard’s “AI Copilot
Recommendation” panel (e.g., Motor-15 bearing wear/shaft misalignment example, 93% confidence, with concrete
inspection and shutdown recommendations).

How the AI Copilot Should Use This Document
When a new anomaly or elevated anomaly score arrives for an asset, the Copilot should:
1. Identify the asset type (Furnace, Conveyor, Slurry Pump, Motor/Drive, Cooling Fan, Crusher/Mill, etc.) and locate the
matching section below.
2. Match the triggered sensor signals (which parameters are out of range, trending, or flagged by the Isolation
Forest) against the Symptom → Probable Root Cause tables in that section.
3. Use the combined anomaly score and rate of change to judge severity and set a Risk Level (Healthy / Warning /
Critical) and Priority (Low / Medium / High / Urgent).
4. Cross-check failure history for the asset (recurring root causes, recent maintenance date) — a symptom that
recurs shortly after a related repair should raise suspicion of incomplete repair or a secondary cause.
5. Generate a Recommendation using the standard output format defined in Section 11, including root cause
candidates with confidence, recommended inspection/action steps, urgency/ETA, and whether a Work Order should
be auto-suggested.
6. Where multiple root causes are plausible, list them ranked by likelihood and give a confidence percentage,
mirroring the dashboard’s “Kemungkinan Penyebab” (Possible Causes) format.

2.2 Anomaly Scoring and Severity Bands
The Anomaly Score (Section 6 of the pipeline) is a normalized 0–100 combination of:
ML anomaly score from Isolation Forest — reflects how far the current multivariate sensor pattern sits from normal
operating clusters learned from historical data.
Rule-based score — reflects how many/how severely fixed thresholds, control limits, or domain rules are breached
(e.g., vibration > ISO 10816 Zone D, temperature > OEM max rating, rate-of-change > X%/hour).
Recommended severity bands (tune per asset class using historical failure data, but use these as defaults):
Health Score
Combined Score Status Meaning Default Action
(dashboard)
0–20 80–100% Healthy Normal operation, normal Continue monitoring, no
variance action
21–45 55–79% Warning Early-stage degradation Schedule inspection within
signature detected days; increase monitoring
frequency
46–70 30–54% Warning/Critical borderline Confirmed degradation Plan corrective
trend, moderate risk of maintenance; generate
failure within weeks Work Order (Medium/High
priority)
71–100 0–29% Critical High risk of imminent failure Generate Work Order
(days or less) immediately (High/Urgent);
consider controlled
shutdown
Rate of change matters as much as absolute value. A parameter that is within normal range but has moved sharply
(e.g., vibration +15% in 48 hours, as in the Motor-15 example) should be flagged even if the absolute value has not yet
crossed a hard threshold, because trend velocity is often the earliest and most reliable predictor of bearing, alignment,
and lubrication failures.
2.3 Confidence Scoring for Root-Cause Recommendations
The Copilot should report a confidence percentage for each candidate root cause, derived from:
Number of corroborating signals (e.g., vibration + temperature both trending together increases confidence versus a
single-signal anomaly).
Similarity to known historical failure signatures for that asset or asset class (pattern match against Failure History
log).

Strength/duration of threshold breach.
Absence of a more likely explanation (e.g., no exclusion by process/context data, such as a known process transient
or planned load change).
As a general rule: - Single weak signal, no history match: 40–60% confidence — recommend inspection only, no
automatic Work Order. - Two or more correlated signals, matches a known signature: 70–90% confidence —
recommend Work Order with specific action. - Multiple strong signals + matches recent recurring failure pattern
in history: 90%+ confidence — recommend urgent Work Order and consider shutdown.

3.3 Furnace-Specific Notes for the Copilot
Furnace anomalies that touch off-gas composition, cooling water loss, or hydraulic/tilt instability during
pouring should always be escalated with Urgent priority regardless of the numeric anomaly score, because they
carry personnel-safety and breakout risk, not just asset-damage risk.
Refractory degradation is progressive and largely irreversible between reline campaigns — the correct
recommendation is usually monitor and plan for the next scheduled shutdown, not an emergency stop, unless
the rate of hot-spot growth is accelerating or approaching the OEM breakout-risk threshold.
Always cross-reference the campaign age (days/hours since last reline) when assessing refractory-related
anomalies — a hot spot appearing near end-of-campaign is expected degradation; the same hot spot early in a
campaign is anomalous and warrants deeper investigation (possible install defect).

4.3 Conveyor-Specific Notes for the Copilot
Because conveyors have many identical idlers, the Copilot should always specify which idler/pulley position the
anomaly relates to (from the sensor tag ID) rather than a generic “the conveyor” recommendation — this is essential
for a technician to act efficiently.
Belt tracking issues that are ignored can progress to belt edge damage or belt walk-off, which is a safety and
major-cost failure mode; tracking anomalies should be escalated proportionally faster (age-to-failure is often short —
hours to days) compared to bearing wear (days to weeks).
Material spillage/buildup is one of the most common and cheapest-to-fix causes of motor current and temperature
anomalies on conveyors — this should generally be checked/ruled out before recommending a bearing or gearbox
teardown.

5.3 Slurry Pump-Specific Notes for the Copilot
Slurry pumps in gold processing typically see continuous abrasive wear as the dominant failure mode (impeller,
liners, throat bush) — this is different from clean-water pump populations, so the Copilot should weight wear-pattern
(gradual pressure/flow decline + rising current) explanations more heavily than in generic pump guidance.
Loss of seal water / gland flush is a high-urgency condition even at a low combined anomaly score, because
consequence (mechanical seal failure, slurry leak, environmental/safety exposure) is severe and fast-developing. The
Copilot should apply a severity override: treat confirmed seal-water loss as Critical/Urgent regardless of the
numeric anomaly score.
Cavitation and blockage produce similar-looking pressure/flow instability; the distinguishing signal is vibration

character (cavitation = high-frequency broadband “gravel” noise) and sump/suction level (cavitation correlates
with low suction level; blockage does not).

6.3 Recommended Output Mirrors the Dashboard Format
For a motor anomaly, the Copilot’s recommendation should be structured exactly like the dashboard’s AI Copilot
Recommendation panel:
Summary line: e.g., “Motor-15 shows a 15% increase in vibration over the last 48 hours.”
Possible causes (ranked): e.g., Bearing wear; Shaft misalignment.
Confidence: single overall percentage (e.g., 93%) reflecting combined signal strength.
Recommendation checklist: concrete, checkable action items, e.g.:
Perform bearing inspection
Check shaft alignment
Add lubrication
Schedule shutdown within N days
Each recommended action should be specific enough to become a Work Order task line directly.
6.4 Motor-Specific Notes for the Copilot
Always check maintenance/failure history first. If the asset’s Failure History log shows a recent bearing
replacement or lubrication event, and the current anomaly is a new/different signature, weight electrical or
misalignment causes higher; if it’s the same signature recurring, weight incomplete repair or wrong root cause on
the prior work order higher.
Bearing wear + misalignment is the most common combined signature in this plant and should be the
default leading hypothesis whenever vibration and temperature rise together without a load change — this matches
observed plant history.
Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimates shown on the dashboard (e.g., “15 Days”) should be treated by the
Copilot as a hard planning constraint: any recommended inspection/repair should be scheduled well within the RUL
window, and Work Order urgency should scale inversely with RUL (RUL < 7 days → Urgent/High priority regardless of
combined anomaly score).

7.3 Cooling Fan-Specific Notes for the Copilot
Cooling fans are frequently a secondary/supporting asset for a primary process (furnace cooling, motor cooling)
— when a cooling fan anomaly is detected, the Copilot should also check whether the primary equipment it cools
is showing early temperature effects, and cross-link the recommendation (e.g., “Cooling Fan-02 degradation may
accelerate Motor-15 thermal stress — prioritize both”).
Loss of cooling airflow on a furnace-adjacent fan should be treated with elevated urgency similar to furnace cooling
water loss (Section 3), due to downstream thermal risk.

End-to-End Decision Workflow for the Copilot
1. Receive anomaly event with combined score, triggered signals, and asset ID.
2. Look up asset type → retrieve the matching section of this document.
3. Match triggered signal pattern against the Symptom → Root Cause table for that asset type.
4. Check Failure History for the asset: recurring pattern, recent related maintenance, campaign/service age.
5. Check for any safety-override conditions (furnace off-gas, seal water loss, cooling water loss, structural/mounting
failure risk) — if present, force Priority = Urgent regardless of computed score.
6. Rank candidate root causes, assign overall confidence.
7. Generate output in the Standard Recommendation Output Format above.
8. Pass to Dashboard for Planner Review; do not bypass human approval except where explicitly configured for auto-
WO on Urgent safety-override conditions per plant policy.

Handling Ambiguity, Conflicting Signals, and False Positives
Single-sensor anomaly with no corroboration: treat as low confidence (≤50%); recommend verification (visual
inspection or sensor check) rather than a full corrective Work Order.
Conflicting signals (e.g., vibration rising but temperature falling): do not force a single explanation — report both
observations and note the pattern doesn’t match a standard signature; recommend inspection to gather more data
rather than guessing.
Anomaly coincides with a known process/operational change (e.g., planned load increase, startup/shutdown
transient, ambient temperature swing): the Copilot should check process/context logs where available and lower
confidence or reclassify as “expected variance” if the anomaly is fully explained by the operational change.
Recurring false positives on the same sensor: if a specific sensor tag repeatedly triggers anomalies that are
subsequently found to have no physical cause on inspection, this should be flagged as a candidate for sensor
recalibration or threshold retuning, and referenced in future recommendations for that tag (“this sensor has a history
of false positives — recommend physical verification before Work Order”).
New/unseen pattern (pure ML flag, no rule match, no history match): report honestly as “unusual pattern
detected, no matching historical signature — recommend manual inspection to characterize” rather than forcing a fit
to an existing root-cause category.

Glossary
Term Meaning
RUL Remaining Useful Life — estimated time until functional failure if no action
is taken
ISO 10816 International standard for evaluating machine vibration severity by zone
(A=good, B=acceptable, C=unsatisfactory, D=unacceptable)
NPSH Net Positive Suction Head — available suction pressure margin for a pump;
insufficient NPSH causes cavitation
MCSA Motor Current Signature Analysis — electrical diagnostic technique for
detecting rotor, stator, and bearing faults from current waveform
CSS Closed Side Setting — crusher gap setting that determines product size
CMMS Computerized Maintenance Management System (e.g., SAP PM) — system
of record for Work Orders and maintenance history
Isolation Forest Unsupervised machine learning algorithm used to detect anomalous
multivariate sensor patterns without labeled failure data
Combined Anomaly Score The weighted/combined output of the ML (Isolation Forest) score and rule-
based threshold score, normalized 0–100

Document Maintenance Note
This knowledge base should be treated as a living document. As the plant’s Failure History log accumulates confirmed root
causes and outcomes, the specific thresholds, confidence weightings, and symptom-pattern tables in this document
should be periodically reviewed and updated (recommended: quarterly) so that the AI Copilot’s recommendations continue
to reflect the plant’s actual failure statistics rather than only generic industry baselines.
